# Proof

**Claim:** Yes. Any orthogonal projection of an ellipsoid $\Delta_{A,c}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ onto a subspace $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ is again an ellipsoid (in $V$).

---

**Setup.** Let $E=\Delta_{A,c}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:x^{T}Ax\le c\}$ with $A$ symmetric positive definite and $c>0$. Let $V\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$ be a subspace with $\dim V=k\ge 1$, and let $P=P_V$ denote orthogonal projection onto $V$. We show $P(E)=\{Px:x\in E\}$ is an ellipsoid in $V$.

**Step 1: Rewrite $E$ as the preimage of a ball.** Since $A$ is symmetric positive definite, it admits a factorization $A=B^{T}B$ with $B$ invertible (e.g. $B=A^{1/2}$). Then

$$x^{T}Ax\le c \iff \|Bx\|^{2}\le c \iff Bx\in \overline{B}(0,\sqrt{c}),$$

so $E=B^{-1}\bigl(\overline{B}(0,\sqrt{c})\bigr)$.

**Step 2: Express the projection as a linear image of a ball.** Substituting $y=Bx$ (a bijection of $\mathbb{R}^n$),

$$P(E)=\{P\,B^{-1}y:\|y\|\le\sqrt{c}\}=L\bigl(\overline{B}(0,\sqrt{c})\bigr),$$

where $L:=P\circ B^{-1}:\mathbb{R}^n\to V$ is linear.

**Step 3: $L$ is surjective onto $V$.** The map $B^{-1}:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is bijective, and $P:\mathbb{R}^n\to V$ is surjective onto $V$. Hence their composition $L=P\circ B^{-1}$ is surjective onto $V$. In particular $LL^{*}:V\to V$ (where $L^{*}:V\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is the adjoint) is symmetric positive definite, hence invertible.

**Step 4: Image of a ball under a surjective linear map is an ellipsoid.** We use the standard fact: if $L:\mathbb{R}^n\to V$ is surjective, then

$$L\bigl(\overline{B}(0,r)\bigr)=\{z\in V:\; z^{T}(LL^{*})^{-1}z\le r^{2}\}.$$

*Proof of the fact.* $z\in L(\overline{B}(0,r))$ iff there exists $y\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with $\|y\|\le r$ and $Ly=z$. Among all solutions of $Ly=z$, the minimum-norm one is $y_{0}=L^{*}(LL^{*})^{-1}z$ (well-defined since $LL^{*}$ is invertible). Its squared norm is

$$\|y_{0}\|^{2}=z^{T}(LL^{*})^{-1}LL^{*}(LL^{*})^{-1}z=z^{T}(LL^{*})^{-1}z.$$

A solution with $\|y\|\le r$ exists iff the minimum-norm solution satisfies $\|y_{0}\|\le r$, i.e. iff $z^{T}(LL^{*})^{-1}z\le r^{2}$. ∎

**Step 5: Conclude.** Applying Step 4 with $r=\sqrt{c}$,

$$P(E)=\{z\in V:\; z^{T}(LL^{*})^{-1}z\le c\}.$$

Since $(LL^{*})^{-1}$ is symmetric positive definite on $V$ and $c>0$, this is precisely an ellipsoid in $V\cong\mathbb{R}^{k}$.

**Explicit form of the matrix.** Using $A=B^{T}B$ so $B^{-1}(B^{-1})^{T}=(B^{T}B)^{-1}=A^{-1}$, and $P^{*}=P$ (orthogonal projection is self-adjoint),

$$LL^{*}=P\,B^{-1}(B^{-1})^{T}P=P\,A^{-1}P\big|_{V},$$

so the projected ellipsoid is

$$P(E)=\Bigl\{z\in V:\; z^{T}\bigl(P\,A^{-1}P\big|_{V}\bigr)^{-1}z\le c\Bigr\}.$$

**Degenerate cases.** If $V=\mathbb{R}^n$, then $P=I$ and $P(E)=E$ itself. If $V=\{0\}$, the projection is $\{0\}$, the trivial ellipsoid in $0$ dimensions. All cases are consistent.

**Conclusion.** Every orthogonal projection of an ellipsoid $\Delta_{A,c}$ onto a subspace $V$ is an ellipsoid in $V$, with the explicit matrix $(P_V A^{-1}P_V|_V)^{-1}$ and the same constant $c$.
